title: Psalm 83: When the Nations Conspire
summary: The psalmist begs God not to stay silent while a coalition of surrounding nations plots to wipe Israel off the map. He names ten enemies, recalls God's victories over Midian, Sisera, and Jabin in the days of the judges, and asks God to scatter the enemies like chaff and cover them with shame. The prayer ends with the hope that they will come to know that the LORD alone is Most High over all the earth.
story: Psalm 83 closes the collection of psalms headed "of Asaph" (Psalms 73 to 83), and it also closes the larger block scholars call the Elohistic Psalter (Psalms 42 to 83), where the general word for God, Elohim, is used far more often than the personal name the LORD (Yahweh). Fittingly, the psalm's last line breaks through to that name: "whose name is the LORD". Book III has been circling one question since Psalm 73: why do the wicked prosper while God's people suffer? Here the question takes its most political form. Israel's very existence is threatened, and the only resource the psalmist has is to remember what God did before and ask him to do it again. The next psalm turns from enemies at the border to longing for God's house.
historical:
The heading names Asaph, the Levite musician whom Chronicles places over temple song in David's day, whose descendants kept his name as a guild of singers. Whether the headings go back to the original authors or were added by later editors is debated; either way, the psalm belongs to the Asaph collection.

No single war in the historical books matches the list of enemies. Many interpreters point to Jehoshaphat's reign in the ninth century BC, when Moab, Ammon, and people from the region of Edom marched against Judah (2 Chronicles 20). The Chronicler says a Levite "of the sons of Asaph" named Jahaziel prophesied deliverance on that occasion (2 Chronicles 20:14), which makes the link attractive. But Psalm 83 names Assyria as backing the alliance, and Assyria was a rising power from the ninth century and dominant in the eighth and seventh, which leads others to a later date. Still others think the list is not a single historical coalition at all but a deliberate roll call of Israel's traditional enemies on every side, ten nations standing for the whole hostile world. The text allows all three readings.
cultural:
The nations are arranged roughly around Israel's borders. Edom, the Ishmaelites, Moab, and the Hagrites lay to the south and east (the Hagrites were a desert people defeated by the eastern tribes in Saul's day, according to 1 Chronicles 5:10). Ammon lay east of the Jordan. Amalek was the old raiding people of the southern desert. Philistia and Tyre held the coast to the west and northwest. Gebal is either the Phoenician port of Byblos in the north or a district of the same name near Edom in the south; scholars are divided. Assyria, far to the northeast, is described as lending its strength (literally its arm) to "the sons of Lot", that is, Moab and Ammon, whose ancestry Genesis 19 traces to Abraham's nephew Lot. Several of these peoples were Israel's own relatives through Esau, Ishmael, and Lot, which sharpens the betrayal.

The historical examples come from the book of Judges. Sisera, commander of the army of Jabin king of Canaan, was routed at the Kishon brook when God sent a storm that bogged down his chariots (Judges 4 and 5). Oreb and Zeeb were Midianite commanders killed after Gideon's victory, and Zebah and Zalmunna were Midianite kings he captured (Judges 7 and 8). Endor lay in the Jezreel region where these battles were fought. In a land with no strong standing army, these stories were Israel's memory that God fights for a weak people. Tumbleweed and chaff were familiar sights: dry thistle heads rolling before the wind and husks blown off the threshing floor.
literary: Psalm 83 is a communal lament, a prayer spoken for the whole people in a time of national danger. It falls into two halves. Verses 1 to 8 describe the threat: an urgent triple plea ("be not silent; be not speechless; be not still"), then the enemies' plot quoted in their own words (verse 4), then the roll call of the alliance, closed by Selah (a musical or liturgical marker whose exact meaning is uncertain). Verses 9 to 18 are the petition: first by historical example (verses 9 to 12), then by a sequence of nature images that intensify from tumbleweed to chaff to forest fire to storm (verses 13 to 15), and finally by the purpose of the whole prayer (verses 16 to 18). The word name frames the psalm. The enemies want "the name of Israel" remembered no more (verse 4); the psalmist asks that shame drive them to "seek Your name" (verse 16); and the psalm ends by declaring the name of the LORD as Most High.

outline.t: A plea for God to break his silence
The enemies plot to erase Israel
The roll call of the alliance
Do to them as you did in the days of the judges
Scatter them like chaff, pursue them with storm
Let them be ashamed and know the LORD is Most High

doctrines.note: The psalm teaches God's people to bring even their fear and anger about their enemies to him in prayer, and to base their plea on what he has done before. Remembering God's past acts is itself a form of asking.
However large the coalition, the psalm's last word is that the LORD alone is Most High over all the earth. The nations' alliance is not the final power in the world.
The enemies plot against "those You cherish" and against God himself. Because Israel is bound to God by covenant, an attack on his people is treated as an attack on him.

words.note: Berit, covenant. In verse 5 the enemies literally cut a covenant against God, which the BSB renders "form an alliance". The word is the same one used for God's covenants with Noah, Abraham, Israel, and David. The irony is deliberate: the nations bind themselves by treaty against the God whose own covenant binds Israel to him.

Shem, name. In the ancient world a name stood for a person's identity, reputation, and continued existence. To blot out a name was to erase a people from memory. The psalm sets the enemies' aim to end Israel's name against God's aim that his own name be known and sought.

Elyon, Most High. An ancient title for God as supreme over every other power, used as early as Genesis 14, where Melchizedek is priest of God Most High. Here it is the psalm's closing claim: not Assyria or any coalition, but the LORD is highest over all the earth.

christ: The link to Christ here is thematic rather than predictive. Psalm 2 had already pictured the nations plotting together against the LORD and his anointed, and the apostles prayed that psalm when they faced threats in Jerusalem (Acts 4:25-27). Psalm 83 belongs to the same pattern: the powers of the world combine against God's people, and God's people cry out for him to act. The New Testament places Jesus at the center of that pattern. He was handed over by an alliance of rulers, Jewish and Roman, and God overturned their verdict by raising him. The psalm's surprising hope in verse 16, that shame might lead the enemies to "seek Your name", also points forward. In the gospel the nations who once stood against Israel are invited to know the name of the LORD, and Jesus teaches his followers to pray for their enemies (Matthew 5:44) rather than only against them.

hard.q: How can a prayer that asks God to destroy and humiliate enemies belong in Scripture?
hard.a:
Psalm 83 is one of the imprecatory psalms, prayers that call down judgment on enemies, and many readers find them troubling beside Jesus' command to love enemies. Several things help. First, the psalmist does not take revenge himself; he hands the matter to God, which is exactly what Paul later urges (Romans 12:19). Second, the enemies here are not personal rivals but a coalition seeking to exterminate a people, and the prayer is for justice against genocide. Third, the psalm's aim is not simply destruction: verse 16 asks that shame lead them to seek God's name, and verse 18 asks that they come to know him. Some interpreters therefore read the prayer as asking for the defeat of the enemies' plans more than their annihilation.

Other Christians emphasize that these prayers belong to an earlier stage of revelation and are to be prayed now in light of the cross, directed against evil itself rather than against people. Others argue that the Psalms give victims words for honest rage and that praying them keeps anger inside a relationship with a just God instead of turning it into personal violence. These readings are not mutually exclusive, and most interpreters combine them.

questions: The psalmist remembers what God did in the days of Gideon and Deborah as the ground for his request. What past acts of God, in Scripture or in your own life, do you lean on when you are afraid?
Verse 16 asks that the enemies' shame lead them to seek God. How does that change the way you might pray about people who oppose or harm you?
The psalm closes with the claim that the LORD alone is Most High over all the earth. Which powers in the world today seem to you to claim that place?
